summary: Most phone fingerprint sensors are capacitive: they read the tiny electrical differences between the ridges and valleys of living skin. After death, blood flow stops, the skin cools, dries and can wrinkle, so the sensor usually cannot read a match, and phones add their own barriers such as asking for the passcode after 48 hours. But it is not impossible: experts say a very recently deceased person's finger can sometimes still work, which is the surprising twist.
audience: Curious Pakistani smartphone users aged 15-35 on Facebook who wonder how everyday tech works

facts.fact: Most smartphone fingerprint sensors identify a finger through electrical conductance rather than by taking a photo.
facts.source: Live Science (Anil Jain, Michigan State University)

facts.fact: A capacitive sensor is a grid of tiny cells; fingerprint ridges touch the sensor and give a stronger electrical reading than the valleys, which leave a small air gap, so the chip builds a map of the print.
Fingerprint expert Anil Jain says it gets more difficult to unlock a phone with fingertips the longer a person has been dead.
Jain explained that without blood flow the fingers can start to wrinkle or shrivel, which changes the print the sensor sees.
facts.source: Live Science / Fortune coverage quoting Anil Jain

facts.fact: Jain also said that if a person has only recently died, it is possible to unlock a phone with their finger.
Scientists are not sure exactly how long after death the skin stops conducting electricity well enough for a sensor.
iPhones ask for the passcode instead of Touch ID if the phone has not been unlocked for more than 48 hours, after a restart, or after five failed fingerprint attempts.
facts.source: Apple Support: If Touch ID isn't working; Apple Platform Security guide

facts.fact: In 2016, US police asked Jain's lab to make 3D-printed fingertip copies from a murder victim's fingerprints to try to unlock his phone.
Your fingerprint pattern itself does not disappear at death; the problem for phone sensors is the skin's changing electrical and physical condition.

avoid: Saying it NEVER works (experts say a recently deceased finger sometimes can)
Any step-by-step advice on unlocking someone else's or a deceased person's phone
Graphic or gory depictions of bodies or severed fingers
Naming specific criminal cases or victims sensationally
Claiming all phones work the same way (optical and ultrasonic sensors also exist)
